COMP90073 Trustworthy Machine Learning · Workshop Week 11

Threat Models, Certified Defences and Backdoor Attacks

Four questions: white-box versus black-box risk, the limits of randomised smoothing, adversarial CAPTCHAs, and a backdoored MNIST classifier you can probe live. Each prerequisite is explained right before it is needed, with a figure you can play with.

clean data, correct behaviour attacker: poison, trigger, perturbation defender: model, certificate, detector second class
Randomised smoothing: noisy copies vote; the ring certifies the smoothed classifier, not the drawn boundary

A2 · Optimised poisons: two nested problems

Choosing the most harmful poison is a bilevel problem: one optimisation nested inside another (slide 7).

Outer problem · the attacker picks the poison
$$\max_{x_c}\ L\big(\mathcal D_{\text{val}};\ w^\star\big)$$
Inner problem · the defender trains on the poisoned data
$$w^\star = \arg\min_{w}\ L\big(\mathcal D_{\text{tr}} \cup \{(x_c, y_c)\};\ w\big)$$
Biggio et al.: move \(x_c\) uphill on the validation error, retrain the SVM, repeat (slides 7–9).1
Three ways to solve it
Biggio et al. (2012)

Victim: support vector machine.

Idea: exact gradient of the validation error from the SVM's optimality conditions.

1 poison pointslides 7–9
Poison Frogs (2018)

Idea: feature collision. The poison looks like a cat but has the target dog's features.

Needs: the victim's feature extractor \(f\).

1 poison if only the last layer trains≈50 if all layers trainslides 10–14
Witches' Brew (2021)

Idea: gradient matching. Poisons push the weights the same way as "label the target as cat".

Works when the victim trains from scratch.

few poisonsslides 15–16

Poison Frogs2 keeps the poison near a base image \(b\) while matching the target \(t\) in feature space:

$$\min_{x}\ \lVert f(x) - f(t)\rVert_2^2 + \beta\,\lVert x - b\rVert_2^2 .$$

Witches' Brew3 aligns the poisons' training gradient with the attacker's desired gradient:

$$\min_{\Delta}\ 1 - \cos\!\Big(\nabla_\theta \mathcal L\big(f_\theta(t), y_{\text{adv}}\big),\ \tfrac{1}{P}\textstyle\sum_{i} \nabla_\theta \mathcal L\big(f_\theta(x_i + \Delta_i), y_i\big)\Big), \qquad \lVert\Delta_i\rVert_\infty \le \epsilon .$$
Attacks on the procedure, with no change to the data
Batch reordering (slide 18)
Same data, attacker-chosen order: one bad epoch can slow or reset learning.
Sponge poisoning (slide 19)
Training pushes activations away from zero, so every prediction costs more energy.
Derivation · Poison Frogs' backward step is a weighted average

Poison Frogs alternates a gradient step on the feature term with an exact step on the pixel term (slide 12). After the forward step gives \(\hat x\), the backward step solves

$$x = \arg\min_{z}\ \tfrac{1}{2\lambda}\lVert z - \hat x\rVert_2^2 + \tfrac{\beta}{2}\lVert z - b\rVert_2^2 .$$

Set the derivative to zero:

$$\tfrac{1}{\lambda}(z - \hat x) + \beta (z - b) = 0 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad z = \frac{\hat x + \lambda\beta\, b}{1 + \lambda\beta}.$$

So every backward step pulls the poison a fixed fraction of the way back to the base image \(b\), which keeps the poison visually close to the base image.

A3 · Backdoor attacks and the two numbers that measure them

A backdoored model behaves normally on clean inputs, and switches to a hidden behaviour when it sees a trigger (slide 20).

Clean pair\((x, y)\)
→
Attacker's function \(g\)add trigger, set \(y_t\)
→
Poisoned pair\((x \oplus \text{trigger},\ y_t)\)
→
Mixed training set\(\mathcal D_c \cup \mathcal D_b\)
→
One modeltwo behaviours

Ordinary training on the mixture learns both behaviours at once (slide 22). Nothing special is needed.

$$\mathcal L = \underbrace{\mathbb E_{(x,y)\sim\mathcal D_c}\big[\ell(f(x), y)\big]}_{\text{normal behaviour}} + \underbrace{\mathbb E_{(x',y')\sim\mathcal D_b}\big[\ell(f(x'), y')\big]}_{\text{hidden behaviour}} .$$
A trigger can be almost anything (slides 23–24)
patcha small squareclean labellabel stays correctphoto filterNashvillewarpWaNetblendfaint noisestripesSIGLLM word or topicBackdoorLLM
How it gets in (slides 21, 25–27)
Scraped web data
Buy an expired domain and serve a poisoned image at the old link. $1000 controls at least 0.01% of every dataset checked (slide 26).4
Downloaded models
A backdoored pre-trained model survives fine-tuning on your own data. Model hubs host millions of models.
Two numbers measure a backdoor (slide 29)5
Clean accuracy (CA) · keep high
$$\text{{CA}} = \frac{{\#\{{f(x) = y\}}}}{{\#\text{{clean test images}}}}$$

High CA: nobody notices.

Attack success rate (ASR) · attacker wants high
$$\text{{ASR}} = \frac{{\#\{{f(x') = y_t\}}}}{{\#\text{{triggered test images}}}}$$

High ASR: the backdoor works.

A5 · Certified robustness by interval bound propagation

Empirical robustness
Adversarial training. Tested only against the attacks we tried; an untried attack may still succeed.
no guarantee
Certified robustness
A proof that no input in the ball of radius \(r\) changes the answer (slide 15).
guarantee
InteractiveThe same model, judged empirically and with a certificate (slide 15)
empirical: test a few attacks per ball
certified: the largest ball proven safe
class Aclass Bbudget ball, radius \(\epsilon\)certified ball, radius \(r\)attack attempt that flips the label, or a region never checked
The boundary has a thin finger reaching towards one class-A point. On the left, eight attack attempts on each ball's edge miss the finger, so that point "passes" the empirical test, although part of its ball (orange) is on the wrong side. On the right, each point gets a certified radius \(r\): a proven lower bound on its distance to the boundary (drawn here as 85% of the true distance, capped at 0.6, because real certificates are conservative). The point next to the finger honestly gets a small ball. A point is certified when \(r \ge \epsilon\); the gap between \(r\) and the true distance is why certified methods give up earlier than attacks do.

Interval bound propagation (IBP) pushes a whole box of inputs through the network, one neuron at a time.8

Input boxeach pixel \([x_i - \epsilon,\ x_i + \epsilon]\)
→
Each neuronsmallest and largest weighted sum
→
ReLUclip the interval at 0
→
Output scorescat range, dog range
→
Certified?\(\min \text{{cat}} > \max \text{{dog}}\)

For one neuron \(z = \sum_i w_i x_i\) with \(x_i \in [l_i, u_i]\), each term is extreme at one end of its interval:

$$z_{\min} = \sum_{i} \min(w_i l_i,\ w_i u_i), \qquad z_{\max} = \sum_{i} \max(w_i l_i,\ w_i u_i).$$
InteractiveThe two-pixel network of slide 17
Pixels are \(0.5 \pm \epsilon\), and the weights are those of slide 17 (written out below the figure). At \(\epsilon = 0.1\) the cat range \([0.6, 1.2]\) stays above the dog range \([0, 0.2]\): certified. The intervals first overlap at \(\epsilon = 1/6\).

The network in the figure is

$$h_1 = x_1 + x_2, \qquad h_2 = x_1 - x_2, \qquad \text{cat} = \operatorname{ReLU}(h_1) - \operatorname{ReLU}(h_2), \qquad \text{dog} = \operatorname{ReLU}(h_2).$$

"Not certified" does not mean "attackable". The worst real input, \(x_1 = 0.5 + \epsilon\) and \(x_2 = 0.5 - \epsilon\), gives cat \(= 1 - 2\epsilon\) and dog \(= 2\epsilon\), so the label only flips at \(\epsilon = 0.25\). The gap between \(1/6\) and \(0.25\) is the looseness of slide 18.

IBP strength
Fast: one forward pass with intervals.
IBP weakness (slide 18)
Loose: it combines worst cases that cannot happen together, so deep networks get intervals too wide to certify. Randomised smoothing (Q2) is the alternative.

A6 · Input preprocessing, detection and guardrails

Three more defences act around the model instead of changing it.

Input
→
PreprocessJPEG, TV, threshold
→
Classifier
→
Detector or guardreject or review
→
Output
Input preprocessing (slide 24)

How: JPEG compression, total-variation minimisation or binary thresholding removes fine detail.

Limit: an adaptive attacker optimises through the transform.

Detection (slide 25)

How: flag out-of-distribution inputs by confidence, feature distance or a trained detector.

Limit: false alarms; adaptive attacks fool both models.

Guardrails and safety training (slides 26–27)

How: guards screen the prompt and the draft; supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and RLHF change the weights.

Limit: unsafe replies remain; safe requests get refused.

"Passing a detector is not a robustness guarantee."Lecture 20, summary (slide 28)

Q4 tries cognitive distillation and outlier detection on a real backdoored model, and shows the loss signal behind anti-backdoor learning.

InteractivePartition and vote: how many poisons can the vote survive?
Each poisoned record lands in one split, so it can flip at most one model's vote. In the worst case every flipped vote moves from "cat" to "dog", so the gap closes by 2 per poison. The prediction is guaranteed while the clean margin is larger than \(2m\). \(K\) is odd here, so the clean vote never ties, and the cat-voting slider starts at a majority.
Derivation · why the vote survives \(m < \text{margin}/2\) poisons

Let \(n_{\text{cat}}\) and \(n_{\text{dog}}\) be the clean vote counts. Each of the \(m\) poisoned records sits in one split, so at most \(m\) models change their vote.

The worst case moves each changed vote from cat to dog, so after poisoning

$$n'_{\text{cat}} \ge n_{\text{cat}} - m, \qquad n'_{\text{dog}} \le n_{\text{dog}} + m .$$

Cat still wins if \(n_{\text{cat}} - m > n_{\text{dog}} + m\), that is

$$m < \frac{n_{\text{cat}} - n_{\text{dog}}}{2}.$$

The text watermark is detected with a one-sided z-test. With \(T\) tokens, green share \(\gamma\) and \(|s|_G\) green tokens:

$$z = \frac{|s|_G - \gamma T}{\sqrt{T\gamma(1-\gamma)}} .$$
InteractiveDetecting a text watermark (slide 18)
token on the secret green listtoken not on the list
The chip positions are illustrative: in the real scheme the green list depends on the key and the previous token. With \(\gamma = 0.5\), human text has about half green tokens by chance. Slide 18 treats a text with 13 green tokens out of 16 (\(z = 2.5\)) as watermarked. Kirchenbauer et al. use the stricter threshold \(z > 4\) to keep false alarms rare. The same green share is far more convincing in a longer text, because \(z\) grows like \(\sqrt T\).
Question 1 · Lecture 18 (black-box attacks) and lecture 20

Q1 · White-box and black-box threat models

Problem statement

Explain the different risk models associated with a white-box and a black-box threat model for evasion attacks, from the perspective of someone deploying a model.

Prerequisite 1.1

The components of a threat model

A threat model states what we assume about the attacker. It has three parts:

  • Goal. For an evasion attack: make a deployed model misclassify a chosen input at test time.
  • Capability. What the attacker may change, for example any \(\delta\) with \(\lVert\delta\rVert_\infty \le \epsilon\).
  • Knowledge. What the attacker knows about the model. This is where white-box and black-box differ.
KnowledgeAttacker seesTypical attacks
White-boxarchitecture, weights, gradients, inputs and outputsFGSM, PGD, C&W: one gradient per step
Black-box, scoresinputs and output probabilitiesestimate gradients from queries (ZOO)18
Black-box, decisionsinputs and the top label onlyboundary walks (Boundary Attack)19
No queriesnothing about this modeltransfer from a surrogate model20
Prerequisite 1.2

Black-box attacks still work: queries and transfer

Hiding the gradient does not remove it. A score-based attacker can estimate each partial derivative with two queries:

$$\frac{\partial \ell}{\partial x_i} \approx \frac{\ell(x + h\,\mathbf e_i) - \ell(x - h\,\mathbf e_i)}{2h}.$$

For a \(d\)-pixel image a full gradient costs \(2d\) queries, and random-direction estimates cost far fewer. A transfer attacker needs no queries at all: an attack crafted on a surrogate model often works on the target too (Q3 measures this).

So black-box access makes attacks more expensive, not impossible. White-box access is the strongest attacker: anything a black-box attacker can do, a white-box attacker can do too.

InteractiveThe same evasion attack with three levels of knowledge
target model's boundarysurrogate's boundarywhite-box pathblack-box (query) pathtransfer path
Drag the starting point; the dotted circle is the budget (an \(\ell_2\) ball in this two-dimensional demo). The white-box attacker follows the true gradient. The black-box attacker estimates it from score queries along random directions: in this smooth example even 2 queries per step give a good enough direction, so it succeeds as often as white-box and only pays in queries. The transfer attacker attacks a surrogate (dashed boundary) and hopes the result also fools the target: it often does, but not always. The success rates are over a fixed grid of 53 start points, independent of the dragged one.
Warm-up exercise · before Question 1

An attacker estimates the gradient of a score-based MNIST model by central differences, one coordinate at a time.

1. How many queries does one full gradient estimate cost?
2. A 10-step PGD attack using these estimates needs how many queries?
3. How many gradient computations does a white-box attacker need for the same 10 steps?
Show solution

\(d = 784\), so one gradient costs \(2 \times 784 = 1568\) queries, and ten steps cost \(15\,680\). The white-box attacker needs 10 back-propagations.

Black-box access raised the cost by about three orders of magnitude, but did not stop the attack. Rate limits help, but a patient attacker, or one with a surrogate, still gets through.

Bridge to the question. Black-box is a statement about the attacker's cost. The question asks which assumption a defender should plan for.

Official answer

Official answer, step by step
  1. Step 1 · White-box

    The attacker has access to the model, its gradients, and both inputs and outputs: almost complete visibility.

    Cheat note

    White-box tools: FGSM and PGD, using

    $$\nabla_x \ell(f_\theta(x), y)$$
  2. Step 2 · Black-box

    The attacker only has access to the inputs and outputs of the model.

    Cheat note

    Black-box tools: query-based gradient estimates and transfer from a surrogate.

  3. Step 3 · Why black-box is not enough for a defender

    Assuming black-box access is not sufficient for security. Queries and transfer attacks still find adversarial examples, and the model's details can leak (stolen weights, an open-source base model, model extraction by queries).

    Cheat note

    Warm-up: black-box raises the cost from 10 gradients to 15 680 queries. It does not make the attack impossible.

  4. Step 4 · The defender's choice

    As a defender, we should almost always assume white-box access. It lets us assess the security of the model under a worst-case assumption about the attacker's access.

    A defence that only holds against black-box attackers is security through obscurity: it fails the moment the model leaks, like the obfuscated-gradient defences of lecture 20, slide 11.

    Cheat note

    Kerckhoffs's principle: a system should stay secure even if everything except the key is public.

Question 2 · Lecture 20, slides 19–23

Q2 · Limits of randomised smoothing, and how to use it in practice

Problem statement

Certified defences using randomised smoothing produce guarantees that adversarial examples do not exist up to a fixed radius. Describe the limitations of these defences. How would you create an operational system that used certified defences to help mitigate the risk of adversarial attacks?

Prerequisite 2.1

The smoothed classifier

Randomised smoothing does not certify the base model \(f\). It builds a new classifier \(g\) that returns the class \(f\) predicts most often under Gaussian noise (slide 19):21

$$g(x) = \arg\max_{c}\ \Pr\big[f(x + \eta) = c\big], \qquad \eta \sim \mathcal N(0, \sigma^2 I).$$

Let \(p_A\) be the probability of the top class \(A\) under the noise. If \(p_A > \tfrac12\), the vote is \(A\).

Prerequisite 2.2

Where the certified radius comes from

The certified radius is (slide 21)

$$R = \sigma\, \Phi^{-1}(p_A),$$

where \(\Phi^{-1}\) is the inverse of the standard normal CDF. Any \(\delta\) with \(\lVert\delta\rVert_2 < R\) leaves \(g(x + \delta) = A\).

Derivation · the radius from the worst-case boundary, in one dimension

We only know one number about \(f\) near \(x\): the noise lands in class \(A\) with probability \(p_A\). Which base classifier makes the vote flip after the shortest move?

The worst case puts all of \(A\)'s mass on one side of a flat boundary, with the attacker moving straight towards it. Measure along that direction. The Gaussian around \(x\) has \(p_A\) of its mass below the boundary at distance \(r\):

$$\Phi\!\left(\frac{r}{\sigma}\right) = p_A \quad\Longrightarrow\quad r = \sigma\,\Phi^{-1}(p_A).$$

Moving the centre by \(\lVert\delta\rVert_2\) towards the boundary leaves \(A\) a share

$$\Phi\!\left(\frac{r - \lVert\delta\rVert_2}{\sigma}\right),$$

which is still above \(\tfrac12\) exactly while \(\lVert\delta\rVert_2 < r\). So \(R = r = \sigma\Phi^{-1}(p_A)\): at that distance the vote is tied (slide 21).

Footnote: the full proof uses the Neyman–Pearson lemma (among all regions with a given probability under one Gaussian, a half-space has the least probability under a shifted Gaussian) to show that the half-space is indeed the worst case. It also handles the runner-up class \(B\):

$$R = \tfrac{\sigma}{2}\big(\Phi^{-1}(\underline{p_A}) - \Phi^{-1}(\overline{p_B})\big),$$

which reduces to the formula above when \(\overline{p_B} = 1 - \underline{p_A}\).

InteractiveSmoothing a curved classifier
noise sample voted \(A\) (cat)noise sample voted \(B\) (dog)certified \(\ell_2\) ball, radius \(R\)an \(\ell_\infty\) ball of the same budget
Drag the input \(x\). The base classifier \(f\) is cat inside the curved region; outside, the top class \(A\) is dog. Points near the boundary get a small radius or none (abstain); with \(n = 20\) copies the margin \(t \approx 0.59\) is so large that every point abstains. The ball may cross \(f\)'s boundary: it protects the smoothed classifier \(g\), whose vote stays \(A\) even when some noisy copies vote the other way. The \(\ell_\infty\) option draws a square of half-side \(R\), whose corners lie \(R\sqrt2\) away, outside the certified ball. A larger \(\sigma\) certifies bigger balls far from the boundary, but blurs the decision near it. The confidence level is fixed at \(\alpha = 0.001\), as in slide 22.
Prerequisite 2.3

Estimating \(p_A\), and when to abstain

We cannot compute \(p_A\); we count votes over \(n\) noisy copies and get \(\hat p_A\) (slide 22). The count could be high by chance, so we subtract a safety margin from Hoeffding's inequality (slide 22):22

$$\Pr\big(\hat p_A - p_A \ge t\big) \le e^{-2nt^2} = \alpha \quad\Longrightarrow\quad t = \sqrt{\frac{\ln(1/\alpha)}{2n}} .$$

Then certify with the "safe guess" of slide 22, a lower confidence bound \(\underline{p_A} = \hat p_A - t\):

$$R = \sigma\, \Phi^{-1}\big(\underline{p_A}\big).$$

The certificate then holds with probability at least \(1 - \alpha\) over the random noise (with \(\alpha = 0.001\), the bound fails at most once in a thousand). If \(\underline{p_A} \le \tfrac12\), the cat might lose the vote, so the procedure abstains (slide 22).

InteractiveRadius against vote share
horizontal: observed share \(\hat p_A\) · vertical: certified radius \(R\)
The dashed curve uses the true share; the solid curve subtracts Hoeffding's margin \(t\). With \(n = 10^5\), \(\hat p_A = 0.9\) and \(\sigma = 0.25\) you get slide 22's numbers. The radius grows with \(\sigma\), but even \(\hat p_A = 0.999\) only gives about \(2.5\sigma\) (\(3.1\sigma\) before the margin).
Prerequisite 2.4

Why the guarantee is an \(\ell_2\) guarantee

The Gaussian is round, so the certificate is a round (\(\ell_2\)) ball. The usual image threat model is an \(\ell_\infty\) box, and in \(d\) dimensions the box's corners are far outside the ball:

$$\lVert\delta\rVert_\infty \le \epsilon \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \lVert\delta\rVert_2 \le \epsilon\sqrt d,$$

with equality at the corners, where every pixel moves by \(\pm\epsilon\). To cover the whole \(\ell_\infty\) box we would need \(R \ge \epsilon\sqrt d\). For MNIST with \(\epsilon = 0.1\) that is \(0.1 \times 28 = 2.8\), far above typical certified radii (slide 22: ImageNet, 49% certified at \(R = 0.5\)).

Warm-up exercise · before Question 2

Use slide 22: \(n = 100\,000\) noisy copies, \(90\,000\) votes for cat, \(\alpha = 0.001\), \(\sigma = 0.25\).

Show solution
$$t = \sqrt{\frac{6.91}{200\,000}} \approx 0.0059, \qquad R = 0.25\,\Phi^{-1}(0.894) \approx 0.25 \times 1.248 = 0.312 .$$

With \(n = 100\): \(t = \sqrt{6.91/200} \approx 0.186\), so \(\underline{p_A} \approx 0.714\) and \(R = 0.25\,\Phi^{-1}(0.714) \approx 0.14\). Fewer copies, a much smaller certificate.

The \(\ell_\infty\) box needs \(R \ge 2.8\): nine times the radius we just certified.

Bridge to the question. Each number points at a limitation: the certificate costs \(10^5\) forward passes, it is an \(\ell_2\) statement, and it is small.

Worked solution: an operational system

A certificate cannot tell whether an input is an attack: an adversarial example also gets a radius. But a small radius means the input is close to the decision boundary, and that is where adversarial examples live. The figure below uses the radius as a triage signal.

InteractiveUsing the certified radius to route inputs to review
clean inputsadversarial inputs (minimal attack on \(f\))review threshold \(\tau\)
horizontal: certified radius \(R\) (abstain counts as \(R = 0\))
Computed live on the two-dimensional classifier above (\(\sigma\) from that figure, \(n = 400\) copies per input). Adversarial inputs are clean points pushed just across the base classifier's boundary. Inputs with \(R < \tau\) go to a human or a slower check. Raising \(\tau\) catches more attacks but sends more clean traffic to review. With \(n = 400\) copies no radius can exceed about \(1.32\sigma\), which is the spike of clean inputs on the right. These attacks stop just across the boundary; an attacker who pushes further gets a large radius and escapes the review, which is why the certificate cannot be used as an alarm on its own.
Official answer, step by step
  1. Step 1 · The threat model is narrow

    Certified defences typically only apply to an \(\ell_2\) norm threat model. Patches, rotations, or an \(\ell_\infty\) attack with the same \(\epsilon\) can lie outside the certified ball.

    Cheat note

    Box corners are far away:

    $$\lVert\delta\rVert_2 \le \epsilon\sqrt d$$
  2. Step 2 · Conservative and expensive

    They are by necessity conservative, and require additional computation to construct the guarantee: about \(10^5\) noisy forward passes per certified input.

    Cheat note

    Hoeffding margin:

    $$t = \sqrt{\ln(1/\alpha)/2n}$$
  3. Step 3 · It certifies a different model

    Crucially, the guarantee is not for the base model \(f\) but for the smoothed model \(g\): the (estimated) most likely class under Gaussian noise. You must deploy \(g\), with its lower clean accuracy, to get the guarantee.

    Cheat note
    $$g(x) = \arg\max_c \Pr[f(x + \eta) = c]$$
  4. Step 4 · A certificate is not an alarm

    An operational system cannot tell from the certificate whether a sample is under attack. The certified radius may be the radius of an adversarial example, which is itself certified as whatever wrong class it landed in.

    Cheat note

    The certificate is about the neighbourhood of the input you were given, not about the clean input it came from.

  5. Step 5 · Use the radius for triage

    But the radius measures how close a sample is to the decision boundary, and samples close to the boundary may be adversarial. Route samples with a small radius, or an abstention, to additional review: a human, a slower ensemble, or a request for more information.

    Cheat note

    Review if

    $$R < \tau \ \text{ or abstain}$$
Question 3 · Lecture 21, slide 24

Q3 · Adversarial perturbations for human-friendly CAPTCHAs

Problem statement

In the lectures it was mentioned that adversarial attacks against CAPTCHA systems have the potential to make the CAPTCHA task more human friendly. How is this possible, and what would be required to do this? Can you think of other systems that can be improved in a similar fashion?

Prerequisite 3.1

Transferability, and the gap between people and models

Two facts from the attack lectures combine here:

  • The perception gap. A small \(\ell_\infty\) perturbation barely changes what a person sees, yet it can change what a model predicts.
  • Transfer. Adversarial examples crafted on one model often fool other models trained for the same task, even with different architectures.20

Old CAPTCHAs fought solvers by distorting the letters, which also hurt people. An adversarial CAPTCHA keeps the letters clear and adds noise that targets solver models instead (slide 24).

A CAPTCHA has several characters, and the solver must read all of them. If it reads each character correctly with probability \(p\), independently, it solves a \(k\)-character CAPTCHA with probability

$$P_{\text{solve}} = p^{k}.$$
Warm-up exercise · before Question 3

A solver reads clean digits with per-character accuracy 0.98, and the CAPTCHA has 4 digits.

1. The probability that the solver passes a clean CAPTCHA:
2. Adversarial noise drops per-character accuracy to 0.6. The new solve rate:
Show solution
$$0.98^4 \approx 0.922, \qquad 0.6^4 \approx 0.130 .$$

A moderate drop per character becomes a large drop per CAPTCHA, because the solver must get every character right. People are unaffected if the noise is small.

Bridge to the question. The second number is roughly what we measure below for a solver the CAPTCHA designer never saw.

Empirical study: attack one solver, test another

We trained two MNIST "solvers" offline: a LeNet (the designer's surrogate) and a fully-connected network (an unseen solver). Each digit gets PGD noise against the LeNet only, then both models read it. 2000 test digits per budget; numbers computed with PyTorch and embedded.

PrecomputedAdversarial digit CAPTCHAs
per-character accuracy against \(\epsilon\)
4-digit solve rate \(p^4\) against \(\epsilon\)
surrogate solver (attacked, LeNet)unseen solver (transfer, MLP)
The unseen solver is hurt less than the attacked one, as transfer theory predicts, but it is still hurt a lot once \(\epsilon \ge 0.15\). On MNIST a faint speckle is already visible at \(\epsilon = 0.05\) and the noise is obvious by \(\epsilon = 0.2\). We did not measure human legibility: finding the largest budget people do not mind is part of the design work.
Official answer, step by step
  1. Step 1 · What is required

    We need access to models designed to defeat CAPTCHA systems. Then we can construct adversarial examples against those models, and a CAPTCHA built from them should defeat them.

    Cheat note

    White-box access to the attacker's solver, or a good surrogate of it.

  2. Step 2 · Why it generalises

    The attack is designed against one or several solver models, but transferability implies it is also likely to work against other, undefended solvers.

    Cheat note

    Measured above: the unseen MLP drops from 95% to 60% per digit at \(\epsilon = 0.2\).

  3. Step 3 · Why it is more human-friendly

    So we can make CAPTCHAs that are harder for machines to read without making them harder for people. The characters no longer need heavy distortion; the difficulty for machines comes from perturbations people barely notice.

    Cheat note
    $$P_{\text{solve}} = p^k$$
  4. Step 4 · The arms race

    Solver models can start to use adversarial defences, such as adversarial training. As the lectures discussed, no guarantee is infallible. But even as the arms race continues, it pushes CAPTCHAs towards stronger noise against machines, not towards letters that are harder for people to read.

    Cheat note

    Slide 30's limitation: solvers can adapt.

  5. Step 5 · Other systems

    The same idea protects people elsewhere (lecture 21):

    • Fawkes cloaks personal photos so face-recognition models learn the wrong face.
    • Unlearnable examples make scraped photos useless as training data.
    • Adversarial clothing hides the wearer from person detectors.
    • Anti-scraping or anti-OCR text, and image cloaks against style mimicry by generative models.
    Cheat note

    Pattern: a perturbation people ignore, aimed at a model people do not want to work.

Q4 · Notebook cells 10–12

4.2 · Trigger injection

The trigger is a filled square of side size and intensity value, placed pad pixels from a chosen corner. Cell 11 writes it into a copy of a \((1, H, W)\) array. For the bottom-left corner the top-left pixel of the square is

$$(r_0, c_0) = (H - \texttt{pad} - \texttt{size},\ \texttt{pad}) = (28 - 1 - 3,\ 1) = (24, 1)$$

for the 3-pixel trigger used in training.

Cell 11Stamp a square trigger
def add_square_trigger_numpy(img: np.ndarray, size: int = 3, value: int = 255, location: str = "bottom_left", pad: int = 1):
    """
    Add a black/white square trigger to a (1,H,W) numpy array in [0,255] uint8.
    - size: side length in pixels
    - value: pixel intensity (0=black, 255=white)
    - location: position of the square ('bottom_left' etc.)
    - pad: offset from the edge
    Returns a modified copy of the image.
    """
    assert img.ndim == 3 and img.shape[0] == 1, "expected (1,H,W)"
    _, H, W = img.shape
    arr = img.copy()

    if location == "bottom_left":
        r0, c0 = H - pad - size, pad
    elif location == "bottom_right":
        r0, c0 = H - pad - size, W - pad - size
    elif location == "top_left":
        r0, c0 = pad, pad
    elif location == "top_right":
        r0, c0 = pad, W - pad - size
    else:
        raise ValueError(f"Unknown location: {location}")

    r1, c1 = r0 + size, c0 + size
    arr[:, r0:r1, c0:c1] = value
    return arr
Cell 12Preview: a 5 × 5 bottom-right trigger
poisoned_imgs = []
for i in range(len(imgs)):
    poisoned_imgs.append(torch.from_numpy(add_square_trigger_numpy(imgs[i].numpy(), size=5, value=255, location="bottom_right", pad=1)))

Worth discussing

Cell 12 previews a 5 × 5 bottom-right trigger, but the attack in cell 16 uses a 3 × 3 bottom-left one. The figure in 4.5 shows why this matters: in our model the trigger succeeds on 99.7% of non-zero digits at the trained bottom-left position and 79% on average within 2 pixels of it, but only 0.5% on average further away.

InteractiveDesign a trigger
The digit is a 7; the readout shows what the backdoored LeNet reads. A square of side \(s\) overwrites \(s^2\) of the 784 pixels. MNIST digits rarely touch the border, so a corner trigger almost never overlaps the stroke, which makes it easy to learn and invisible to a quick look.
Q4 · Notebook cells 13–16

4.3 · The poisoned dataset

Cell 15 subclasses torchvision.datasets.MNIST and overwrites self.data and self.targets in place, so every later read sees the poisoned images. This simulates a dataset that was tampered with before you downloaded it.

Indices are chosen with random.Random(seed).sample, so the same seed always poisons the same images:

$$n_{\text{poison}} = \operatorname{round}(0.02 \times 60\,000) = 1200 .$$
Cell 15InMemoryPoisonedMNIST
# Cell: InMemoryPoisonedMNIST - subclass of torchvision.datasets.MNIST
from typing import Optional, Dict, Any, Sequence
import os
import json
import random
import numpy as np
import torch
from torchvision.datasets import MNIST

class InMemoryPoisonedMNIST(MNIST):
    """
    Subclass of torchvision.datasets.MNIST that can apply an *in-memory*
    deterministic data-poisoning modification to the dataset tensors.

    After calling `apply_poison(...)` the underlying `self.data` and `self.targets`
    are modified (uint8 images in `self.data` are overwritten in-place).
    This simulates a dataset that was downloaded already poisoned.

    Parameters
    ----------
    root : str
        dataset root passed to MNIST
    train : bool
        train or test split (poisoning typically applied to train=True)
    download : bool
        whether to download
    """
    def __init__(self, root: str = "./data", train: bool = True, download: bool = True, **kwargs):
        super().__init__(root=root, train=train, download=download, **kwargs)
        # internal bookkeeping
        self.poisoned_indices: Optional[Sequence[int]] = None
        self.poison_metadata: Optional[Dict[str, Any]] = None
        # keep a small in-memory copy if user wants to be able to restore later
        self._orig_data = None
        self._orig_targets = None

    def _compute_coords(self, H: int, W: int, size: int, location: str, pad: int):
        """Helper: compute (r0,r1,c0,c1) for square given image HxW."""
        s = int(size)
        if location == "bottom_left":
            r0, c0 = H - pad - s, pad
        elif location == "bottom_right":
            r0, c0 = H - pad - s, W - pad - s
        elif location == "top_left":
            r0, c0 = pad, pad
        elif location == "top_right":
            r0, c0 = pad, W - pad - s
        elif location == "center":
            r0, c0 = (H - s) // 2, (W - s) // 2
        else:
            raise ValueError(f"Unknown location: {location}")
        r1, c1 = r0 + s, c0 + s
        # clamp
        r0, r1 = max(0, r0), min(H, r1)
        c0, c1 = max(0, c0), min(W, c1)
        return r0, r1, c0, c1

    def apply_poison(
        self,
        p_poison: float = 0.02,
        target_label: int = 0,
        size: int = 3,
        value: int = 255,
        location: str = "bottom_left",
        pad: int = 1,
        seed: int = 42,
        overwrite: bool = True,  # kept for API compatibility (no-op here)
        save_indices_path: Optional[str] = None,
        save_metadata_path: Optional[str] = None,
        keep_original_copy: bool = False,
    ) -> Dict[str, Any]:
        """
        Apply in-memory poisoning using add_square_trigger_numpy on (1,H,W) arrays.
        """
        assert 0.0 <= p_poison <= 1.0, "p_poison must be in [0,1]"
        n = len(self.data)
        n_poison = int(round(p_poison * n))
        rng = random.Random(seed)
        poisoned_idx = sorted(rng.sample(range(n), n_poison))

        # optional backup
        if keep_original_copy and (self._orig_data is None):
            self._orig_data = self.data.clone()
            self._orig_targets = self.targets.clone()

        # ensure tensor types
        if not isinstance(self.data, torch.Tensor):
            self.data = torch.tensor(self.data, dtype=torch.uint8)
        else:
            # work on CPU uint8
            if self.data.dtype != torch.uint8:
                self.data = (self.data.clone() * 255).to(torch.uint8)
            if self.data.device.type != "cpu":
                self.data = self.data.cpu()

        if not isinstance(self.targets, torch.Tensor):
            self.targets = torch.tensor(self.targets)

        # apply trigger via numpy helper per selected index
        for idx in poisoned_idx:
            # self.data[idx]: [H, W] uint8
            hw = self.data[idx].numpy()                                # (H, W), uint8 (shared mem view)
            chw = hw[None, ...]                                        # (1, H, W)
            poisoned = add_square_trigger_numpy(
                chw, size=size, value=value, location=location, pad=pad
            )                                                          # (1, H, W), uint8
            self.data[idx] = torch.from_numpy(poisoned[0])             # back to [H, W] uint8
            self.targets[idx] = int(target_label)

        metadata = {
            "n_total": n,
            "n_poison": n_poison,
            "p_poison": float(p_poison),
            "target_label": int(target_label),
            "trigger": {"size": int(size), "value": int(value), "location": location, "pad": int(pad)},
            "seed": int(seed),
            "poisoned_indices": poisoned_idx,
        }
        self.poisoned_indices = poisoned_idx
        self.poison_metadata = metadata

        if save_indices_path is not None:
            np.save(save_indices_path, np.array(poisoned_idx, dtype=np.int32))
        if save_metadata_path is not None:
            with open(save_metadata_path, "w") as f:
                json.dump(metadata, f, indent=2)

        return metadata

    def restore_original(self):
        """
        Restore original data/targets if keep_original_copy=True was used.
        """
        if self._orig_data is None or self._orig_targets is None:
            raise RuntimeError("No original copy stored. Create with keep_original_copy=True in apply_poison().")
        self.data = self._orig_data.clone()
        self.targets = self._orig_targets.clone()
        self.poisoned_indices = None
        self.poison_metadata = None

Q4 · Notebook cells 17–22

4.4 · Training and evaluation

Cell 18LeNet-5 style network
import torch
import torch.nn as nn
import torch.nn.functional as F
from torch.utils.data import DataLoader
from typing import Tuple, Optional

# -------------------------
# LeNet-5 style model
# -------------------------
class LeNet(nn.Module):
    """
    LeNet-5 style convnet adapted for MNIST (1x28x28 input).
    Architecture (classic):
      Conv1(1->6, kernel=5) -> ReLU -> AvgPool(2)
      Conv2(6->16, kernel=5) -> ReLU -> AvgPool(2)
      Flatten -> FC(16*4*4 -> 120) -> ReLU
             -> FC(120 -> 84) -> ReLU
             -> FC(84 -> num_classes)
    """
    def __init__(self, num_classes: int = 10):
        super().__init__()
        self.conv1 = nn.Conv2d(1, 6, kernel_size=5)      # 28 -> 24
        self.pool1 = nn.AvgPool2d(kernel_size=2, stride=2)  # 24 -> 12
        self.conv2 = nn.Conv2d(6, 16, kernel_size=5)     # 12 -> 8
        self.pool2 = nn.AvgPool2d(kernel_size=2, stride=2)  # 8 -> 4

        self.fc1 = nn.Linear(16 * 4 * 4, 120)
        self.fc2 = nn.Linear(120, 84)
        self.fc3 = nn.Linear(84, num_classes)

        # optional small init (closer to original LeNet)
        for m in self.modules():
            if isinstance(m, nn.Conv2d):
                nn.init.kaiming_normal_(m.weight, nonlinearity='relu')
                if m.bias is not None:
                    nn.init.zeros_(m.bias)
            elif isinstance(m, nn.Linear):
                nn.init.kaiming_uniform_(m.weight, nonlinearity='relu')
                if m.bias is not None:
                    nn.init.zeros_(m.bias)
    
    def forward_features(self, x: torch.Tensor) -> torch.Tensor:
        x = F.relu(self.conv1(x))
        x = self.pool1(x)
        x = F.relu(self.conv2(x))
        x = self.pool2(x)
        x = x.view(x.shape[0], -1)
        x = F.relu(self.fc1(x))
        return x

    def forward(self, x: torch.Tensor) -> torch.Tensor:
        x = self.forward_features(x)
        x = F.relu(self.fc2(x))
        x = self.fc3(x)  # logits
        return x

Shapes through the network, for one \(1 \times 28 \times 28\) image:

$$28 \xrightarrow{\ 5\times5\ } 24 \xrightarrow{\ \text{pool}\ } 12 \xrightarrow{\ 5\times5\ } 8 \xrightarrow{\ \text{pool}\ } 4, \qquad 16 \times 4 \times 4 = 256 \to 120 \to 84 \to 10 .$$

forward_features returns the 120-dimensional output of fc1. Sections 4.6 and 4.7 use it as the feature space.

Cell 20Meters, accuracy, evaluate and train
from tqdm import tqdm

class AverageMeter(object):
    """Computes and stores the average and current value"""

    def __init__(self):
        self.reset()

    def reset(self):
        self.val = 0
        self.avg = 0
        self.sum = 0
        self.count = 0
        self.max = 0

    def update(self, val, n=1):
        self.val = val
        self.sum += val * n
        self.count += n
        self.avg = self.sum / self.count
        self.max = max(self.max, val)

def accuracy(output, target, topk=(1,)):
    maxk = max(topk)

    batch_size = target.size(0)
    _, pred = output.topk(maxk, 1, True, True)
    pred = pred.t()
    correct = pred.eq(target.view(1, -1).expand_as(pred))

    res = []
    for k in topk:
        correct_k = correct[:k].float().sum()
        res.append(correct_k.mul_(1/batch_size))
    return res

@torch.no_grad()
def evaluate(model, eval_data_loader):
    model.eval()
    # Training Evaluations
    loss_meters = AverageMeter()
    acc_meters = AverageMeter()
    loss_list, correct_list = [], []
    for i, data in enumerate(eval_data_loader):
        # Prepare batch data
        images, labels = data
        images = images.to(device, non_blocking=True)
        labels = labels.to(device, non_blocking=True)
        batch_size = images.shape[0]
        logits = model(images)
        loss = F.cross_entropy(logits, labels, reduction='none')
        loss_list += loss.detach().cpu().numpy().tolist()
        loss = loss.mean().item()
        # Calculate acc
        acc = accuracy(logits, labels, topk=(1,))[0].item()

        # Update Meters
        loss_meters.update(loss, batch_size)
        acc_meters.update(acc, batch_size)

        _, predicted = torch.max(logits.data, 1)
        correct = (predicted == labels)
        correct_list += correct.detach().cpu().numpy().tolist()
    stats = {   
        "eval_loss": loss_meters.avg,
        "eval_acc": acc_meters.avg,
        "eval_loss_list": loss_list,
        "eval_correct_list": correct_list,
    }
    return stats


def train(model, optimizer, train_loader):

    # Set Meters
    loss_meters = AverageMeter()
    acc_meters = AverageMeter()

    # Training
    model.train()
    pbar = tqdm(train_loader)
    for i, data in enumerate(pbar):
        # Prepare batch data
        images, labels = data
        images = images.to(device, non_blocking=True)
        labels = labels.to(device, non_blocking=True)
        batch_size = images.shape[0]
        model.zero_grad()
        optimizer.zero_grad()

        # Objective function
        logits = model(images)
        loss = F.cross_entropy(logits, labels)
        
        # Optimize
        loss.backward()
        optimizer.step()
        # Calculate acc
        loss = loss.item()
        acc = accuracy(logits, labels, topk=(1,))[0].item()

        # Update Meters
        loss_meters.update(loss, batch_size)
        acc_meters.update(acc, batch_size)
        pbar.set_postfix(loss=loss, acc=acc*100)

    stats = {
        "train_loss": loss_meters.avg,
        "train_acc": acc_meters.avg,
    }

    return stats

Prerequisite 4.1

Clean accuracy and attack success rate, measured correctly

Cell 21 stamps the trigger on every test image and relabels all of them as 0, so evaluate on that loader reports the share predicted as 0. That includes the 980 test images that really are zeros, which count as "successes" even with no backdoor at all.

The ASR should only count images whose true class is not the target:

$$\text{ASR} = \frac{\#\{\, f(x') = y_t \text{ and } y \ne y_t \,\}}{\#\{\, y \ne y_t \,\}} .$$

This explains the notebook's epoch-1 "ASR" of 10.39%: it is roughly the share of zeros in the test set (9.8%) and means the backdoor had not been learned yet.

Warm-up exercise · before the evaluation

The test set has 10 000 images, 980 of them zeros.

1. How many training images are poisoned?
2. A backdoor-free model predicts 0 for every true zero and for nothing else. What ASR does the notebook's measure report for it?
3. The notebook reports 98.76% at epoch 5. Assuming all true zeros were predicted 0, the corrected ASR is:
Show solution

\(0.02 \times 60\,000 = 1200\). A backdoor-free model scores \(980 / 10\,000 = 0.098\) on the notebook's measure.

$$\text{ASR} = \frac{9876 - 980}{10\,000 - 980} = \frac{8896}{9020} \approx 0.9863 .$$

At epoch 5 the correction is small. At epoch 1 it changes the story: 10.39% is almost entirely true zeros (our re-run: 10.5% versus a corrected 0.8%).

Bridge to the question. The figure below plots both measures for every epoch of our re-run.

Q4 · Notebook cells 26–29 · Lecture 21, slides 10–11

4.7 · Detecting poisons as outliers

Prerequisite 4.2

k-distance and the simplified local outlier factor

Let \(\operatorname{k-dist}(q)\) be the distance from \(q\) to its \(k\)-th nearest neighbour, and \(\operatorname{NN}_k(q)\) its \(k\) nearest neighbours. The lecture's SLOF compares \(q\)'s neighbourhood radius with its neighbours' radii (slide 10):11

$$\operatorname{SLOF}(q) = \frac{1}{k}\sum_{o\,\in\,\operatorname{NN}_k(q)} \frac{\operatorname{k-dist}(q)}{\operatorname{k-dist}(o)} .$$

About 1 means "as crowded as my neighbours"; much larger than 1 means outlier. It is a simplified local outlier factor.24

The notebook's slof function computes something simpler: the mean distance to the \(k\) nearest neighbours, with no ratio:

$$s(q) = \frac{1}{k}\sum_{o\,\in\,\operatorname{NN}_k(q)} \lVert f(q) - f(o)\rVert_2 .$$
InteractiveNeighbourhoods of a clean point and a poisoned point
clean featurespoisoned features\(\operatorname{k-dist}(q)\)\(\operatorname{k-dist}(o)\) of each neighbour
Drag \(q\) (it starts among the four tightly packed poisons). With \(k \le 4\) all its neighbours are poisons, and both scores look normal. At \(k = 5\) one clean point enters the neighbour list, so the notebook's score \(s(q)\) jumps, but \(\operatorname{SLOF}(q)\) stays below 1: the other poisons had to stretch their own k-distance even further to reach clean data. Only at \(k = 6\), when a second clean point enters, does the ratio rise above 1. A tight group of poisons hides from the ratio more easily than from the plain distance, which matches the AUCs measured below.
Cell 27Pairwise distances and the SLOF score
# -------------------------
# Pairwise distance excluding self
# -------------------------
def get_pair_wise_distance(
    data: torch.Tensor,
    reference: torch.Tensor,
    compute_mode: str = "donot_use_mm_for_euclid_dist",
) -> torch.Tensor:
    """
    Compute pairwise L2 distances between `data` and `reference` (NxD vs MxD),
    returning an array of shape [N, M-1] when data is reference (self-distances removed),
    or [N, M] otherwise.

    If `data is reference` (same object), self-distances are removed row-wise.
    """
    assert data.dim() == 2 and reference.dim() == 2, "Expected [N,D] and [M,D] tensors"
    assert data.size(1) == reference.size(1), "Feature dims must match"

    r = torch.cdist(data, reference, p=2, compute_mode=compute_mode)  # [N,M]

    if data.data_ptr() == reference.data_ptr() and data.shape[0] == reference.shape[0]:
        # Same underlying tensor -> remove diagonal entries
        N = r.size(0)
        # Prefer diagonal_scatter if available, else fall back to fill_diagonal_
        try:
            mask = torch.zeros_like(r, dtype=torch.bool)
            mask = torch.diagonal_scatter(mask, torch.ones(N, dtype=torch.bool, device=r.device))
        except AttributeError:
            # Older PyTorch: set diagonal to +inf, then filter later
            r.fill_diagonal_(float("inf"))
            # Now we can just sort/select without explicit masking
            return r
        # Mask out diagonal and reshape to [N, M-1]
        r = r[~mask].view(N, -1)

    return r  # [N,M] or [N,M-1] depending on case


# -------------------------
# Simple Local Outlier Factor (SLOF) score
# -------------------------
@torch.no_grad()
def slof(
    f: torch.Tensor,
    k: int = 16,
    compute_mode: str = "donot_use_mm_for_euclid_dist",
) -> torch.Tensor:
    """
    Compute SLOF scores for feature matrix `f` (N x D).

    SLOF here = mean distance to the k nearest neighbors (excluding self).

    Args:
        f: [N, D] feature tensor (float). Put it on the desired device.
        k: number of nearest neighbors to average.
        normalize: if True, L2-normalize features along dim=1 before scoring.
        compute_mode: forwarded to torch.cdist.
        chunk_size: if set (e.g., 2048), compute distances in chunks to reduce memory.

    Returns:
        score: [N] tensor, higher means more outlier-like.
    """
    assert f.dim() == 2, "f must be [N, D]"
    N = f.size(0)
    if N <= 1:
        return torch.zeros(N, device=f.device)

    # Ensure k is valid (max neighbors excluding self)
    k_eff = max(1, min(k, N - 1))

    # Compute full cdist once
    dist = get_pair_wise_distance(f, f, compute_mode=compute_mode)  # [N, N-1] (or [N,N] if fallback path)
    if dist.shape[1] == N:  # fallback path where diagonal was set to +inf
        # Sort then take the first k_eff finite neighbors
        dist, _ = torch.sort(dist, dim=1)
        score = dist[:, :k_eff].mean(dim=1)
        return score
    # Normal path
    dist, _ = torch.sort(dist, dim=1)  # ascending
    score = dist[:, :k_eff].mean(dim=1)
    return score
Cell 28Score every training sample

Q4 · Notebook cells 30–33 · Lecture 21, slides 8–9

4.8 · Cognitive distillation

Prerequisite 4.3

The smallest pattern that keeps the output

Cognitive distillation learns a mask \(m \in [0,1]^{H \times W}\) per image. It keeps the masked pixels and replaces the rest by noise \(\delta\):

$$x_{cp} = x \odot m + (1 - m) \odot \delta .$$

It minimises the change in output plus the mask's size and roughness (slide 8):10

$$\min_m\ \lVert f(x) - f(x_{cp})\rVert_1 + \alpha\,\lVert m\rVert_1 + \beta\,\operatorname{TV}(m).$$

To keep the mask in \([0,1]\), it is parameterised through a free variable \(w\):

$$m = \tfrac12\big(\tanh(w) + 1\big).$$

The code calls the sparsity weight \(\alpha\) gamma (0.05 in cell 31). The lecture's finding: a backdoored image keeps its output with a much smaller mask, because the trigger alone decides the answer.

Cell 30Total variation and CognitiveDistillation
def total_variation_loss(img, weight=1):
    b, c, h, w = img.size()
    tv_h = torch.pow(img[:, :, 1:, :]-img[:, :, :-1, :], 2).sum(dim=[1, 2, 3])
    tv_w = torch.pow(img[:, :, :, 1:]-img[:, :, :, :-1], 2).sum(dim=[1, 2, 3])
    return weight*(tv_h+tv_w)/(c*h*w)


class CognitiveDistillation(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, lr=0.1, p=1, gamma=0.01, beta=1.0, num_steps=100, mask_channel=1, norm_only=False):
        super(CognitiveDistillation, self).__init__()
        self.p = p
        self.gamma = gamma
        self.beta = beta
        self.num_steps = num_steps
        self.l1 = torch.nn.L1Loss(reduction='none')
        self.lr = lr
        self.mask_channel = mask_channel
        self.get_features = False
        self._EPSILON = 1.e-6
        self.norm_only = norm_only

    def get_raw_mask(self, mask):
        mask = (torch.tanh(mask) + 1) / 2
        return mask

    def forward(self, model, images):
        model.eval()
        if torch.min(images) < 0 or torch.max(images) > 1:
            raise('images should be normalized')
        b, c, h, w = images.shape
        mask = torch.ones(b, self.mask_channel, h, w).to(images.device)
        mask_param = nn.Parameter(mask)
        optimizerR = torch.optim.Adam([mask_param], lr=self.lr, betas=(0.1, 0.1))
        logits = model(images).detach()
        for step in range(self.num_steps):
            optimizerR.zero_grad()
            mask = self.get_raw_mask(mask_param).to(images.device)
            x_cp = images * mask + (1-mask) * torch.rand(b, c, 1, 1).to(images.device)
            adv_logits = model(x_cp)
            loss = self.l1(adv_logits, logits).mean(dim=1)
            norm = torch.norm(mask, p=self.p, dim=[1, 2, 3])
            norm = norm * self.gamma
            loss_total = loss + norm + self.beta * total_variation_loss(mask)
            loss_total.mean().backward()
            optimizerR.step()
        mask = self.get_raw_mask(mask_param).detach().cpu()
        return mask.detach()

Worth discussing
  • The direction of the score depends on the settings. The lecture flags small masks. With the notebook's sparsity weight, most clean masks vanish and poisoned masks keep the trigger, so large masks are flagged. Always check which way the score points before computing an AUC.
  • Cell 30 has a bug in its input check: raise('images should be normalized') raises a string, which Python rejects with TypeError: exceptions must derive from BaseException. It should be raise ValueError(...).
  • Cell 32 runs 200 optimisation steps for every one of the 60 000 images, about \(1.2\times10^7\) forward and backward passes. Our re-run scored all 1200 poisons plus a random 3000 clean images instead.
Q4 · Notebook cell 34

4.9 · Take-home challenges

The notebook ends with three optional challenges. Pointers from this week's lecture for each:

  1. A stealthier trigger. Blended or low-contrast triggers, warps (WaNet) and faint stripes (SIG) from lecture 19, slide 23. Measure CA, ASR and the detection AUC of 4.7–4.8 together; the intensity curve in 4.5 shows the trade-off directly.
  2. Better detection. Track each sample's loss over the first epochs (anti-backdoor learning; the right panel of 4.4 shows the signal appears in epoch 2 here), or use a class-conditional outlier score so poisons are compared with real zeros.
  3. Recover or remove the trigger. Neural Cleanse: for each class \(c\), find the smallest mask and pattern that sends every input to \(c\), and flag a class whose mask is unusually small (lecture 21, slide 12). Then fine-tune, prune or unlearn, and re-measure CA and ASR (slide 15).
Wrap-up

Notes on the notebook

Points worth raising in the tutorial, found while re-running the notebook:

  1. The ASR counts true zeros as successes. Cell 21 relabels every triggered test image as 0, including the 980 real zeros. The epoch-1 "ASR" of 10.39% is mostly those zeros; restricted to non-zero digits it is under 1%. At epoch 5 the correction is small (98.76% becomes about 98.6%).
  2. Cell 12 previews a different trigger (5 × 5, bottom right) from the one used to poison (3 × 3, bottom left). The learned backdoor is position-specific: 99.7% at the trained position, 79% on average within 2 pixels of it, 0.5% further away.
  3. The slof function is a k-NN mean distance, not the lecture's SLOF ratio, and its docstring lists normalize and chunk_size arguments that do not exist. Cell 28 scores within each unshuffled batch of 256. In our re-run: AUC 0.838 per batch, 0.831 over all samples, 0.617 for the true SLOF ratio.
  4. Cognitive distillation's score points the other way from the lecture. With gamma=0.05, most clean masks collapse to nearly zero, and poisoned masks keep the trigger (mean \(\lVert m\rVert_1\) 18.1 versus 3.6). The large-mask direction gives AUC 0.915 in our re-run (0.942 in the notebook).
  5. raise('images should be normalized') in cell 30 raises a TypeError instead of the intended message.
  6. Subclassing MNIST changes the data folder. torchvision names the raw folder after the class, so InMemoryPoisonedMNIST downloads a second copy of MNIST into ./data/InMemoryPoisonedMNIST/raw.
  7. Unused or inconsistent settings: batch_size = 128 in cell 21 is never used (the loaders use 64 and 256); t-SNE's n_iter is renamed max_iter in recent scikit-learn; the t-SNE compares different clean and poisoned images rather than matched pairs.
  8. Cell 31 has no saved output or execution count (it was probably cleared), so its mask figures are missing; this page shows them from our re-run.
  9. Cell 34 ends with leftover chat-assistant text ("If you'd like, I can … Which challenge should we try first?").
Wrap-up

Summary of key results

TopicKey formula or ruleTake-away
Threat model (Q1)white-box: gradients; black-box: \(2d\) queries per gradient, or transferdefend against white-box: the worst case
Smoothed classifier\(g(x) = \arg\max_c \Pr[f(x + \eta) = c]\), \(\eta \sim \mathcal N(0, \sigma^2 I)\)the certificate is for \(g\), not \(f\)
Certified radius\(R = \sigma\,\Phi^{-1}(\hat p_A - t)\), \(t = \sqrt{\ln(1/\alpha)/2n}\)\(\ell_2\) only; abstain if \(\hat p_A - t \le \tfrac12\)
\(\ell_\infty\) versus \(\ell_2\)\(\lVert\delta\rVert_2 \le \epsilon\sqrt d\)MNIST, \(\epsilon = 0.1\): need \(R \ge 2.8\)
Operational use (Q2)review if \(R < \tau\) or abstainsmall radius = near the boundary = suspicious
Adversarial CAPTCHA (Q3)\(P_{\text{solve}} = p^k\); attack a surrogate solver, rely on transferharder for machines, not for people
Backdoor metrics\(\text{CA}\) on clean data; \(\text{ASR}\) on triggered non-target datare-run: CA 98.5%, ASR 98.9%
IBP\(z_{\min} = \sum_i \min(w_i l_i, w_i u_i)\), then ReLUfast, but loose with depth
Partition and votesurvives \(m < (n_{\text{cat}} - n_{\text{dog}})/2\) poisonsone poison corrupts one vote
SLOF\(\tfrac1k \sum_{o} \operatorname{k-dist}(q)/\operatorname{k-dist}(o)\)poisons are outliers only if \(k\) exceeds their cluster
Cognitive distillation\(\min_m \lVert f(x) - f(x_{cp})\rVert_1 + \alpha\lVert m\rVert_1 + \beta\operatorname{TV}(m)\)masks find the trigger; check the score's direction
